Teeth
tēth
n. pl. (plural of tooth; rendering Hebrew shen, Greek odous)
Plural of tooth, from the Saxon toth, formed like feet and geese by vowel change. Hebrew shen is a tooth and also an ivory or a sharp crag, and the law of retaliation — tooth for tooth — uses it as the measure of exact and limited justice.

Biblical Definition

Teeth in Scripture figure violence, extremity, and finally judgment. As weapons they belong to the wicked and to the beasts, and the Psalmist prays for God to disarm them: “thou hast smitten all mine enemies upon the cheek bone; thou hast broken the teeth of the ungodly” (Psalm 3:7) — breaking the teeth is not cruelty but the drawing of a predator's fangs. Job gives the language its most quoted phrase for narrow survival: “My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth” (Job 19:20). Proverbs uses teeth for the small persistent irritation of an unreliable man: “As vinegar to the teeth, and as smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to them that send him” (Proverbs 10:26). Their gravest use is our Lord's. Six times in the Gospels he describes the place of judgment as one of “weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8:12), and gnashing in Scripture is the sound of rage rather than of remorse — Stephen's murderers gnashed on him with their teeth. Hell in Christ's own account is not repentance at last but hostility unended, which is why it is eternal.

Webster 1828 Definition

Plural of tooth. Figures the weapons of the violent, the narrowest escape (the skin of my teeth), and above all the judgment our Lord names weeping and gnashing of teeth.

expand to see more

TEETH, n. plural of tooth. [Sax. toth.] The bony processes in the jaws, used for biting and chewing.

2. The teeth of a saw, comb, or wheel; anything resembling a tooth in form or use.

3. To cast in one's teeth, to reproach or upbraid.

4. The law of retaliation; as, an eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth, Exod. 21.

5. In Scripture, of judgment; as, there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, Matt. 8.

Key Scripture

Psalm 3:7 — "Arise, O LORD; save me, O my God: for thou hast smitten all mine enemies upon the cheek bone; thou hast broken the teeth of the ungodly."

Job 19:20 — "My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth. and"

Matthew 8:12 — "But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth."

Proverbs 10:26 — "As vinegar to the teeth, and as smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to them that send him."

Modern Corruption

Hell is widely reimagined as annihilation, or as remedial, or as a metaphor. Our Lord described it more often than anyone in Scripture, and his repeated image is weeping and gnashing of teeth — grief joined to unbroken rage.

expand to see more

Annihilationism, universalism, and the post-mortem second chance all soften the same texts, and all founder on the words of Christ. He is the one who speaks most about the place, and the phrase he repeats is not merely sorrowful but hostile: gnashing of teeth is what the enemies of Stephen did in Acts 7 while they stoned him, and what the wicked do against the righteous in Psalm 37. The lost in our Lord's descriptions are not penitents held back from a mercy they now desire; they are still gnashing.

That observation answers the most common objection to eternal punishment, which asks how a finite life can deserve an unending penalty. Matthew 8:12 suggests the sin does not stop. The principle to recover is that our Lord's own severity is the measure here, and no doctrine of hell is safe that is gentler than his words. The same mouth that said weeping and gnashing of teeth also said come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and the two are not in competition; the warning is the reason the invitation is urgent.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shen is a tooth, an ivory, or a sharp crag, and appears in the law of exact retaliation. Greek odous is a tooth and brugmos is the gnashing or grinding of them, the noun our Lord uses of judgment.

expand to see more

Hebrew shen (H8127) — tooth, ivory, crag; the measure in tooth for tooth.

Hebrew charaq (H2786) — to gnash or grind the teeth; what the wicked do against the just.

Hebrew malteah (H4973) — the great teeth or jaw teeth; break out the great teeth of the young lions.

Greek odous (G3599) — a tooth; used in the retaliation formula and in the judgment phrase.

Greek brugmos (G1030) — a gnashing, a grinding; joined to weeping in our Lord's descriptions of hell.

Usage

"Of God disarming the violent: thou hast broken the teeth of the ungodly (Psalm 3:7)."

"Of the narrowest escape: I am escaped with the skin of my teeth (Job 19:20)."

"Of the place of judgment: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 8:12)."
